relationship: narrative example of intimate disclosure followed by lost strength
rationale: Sirach warns against surrendering oneself so that a woman overcomes one's strength; Samson's disclosure to Delilah is followed by the loss of his strength and capture, without making every relationship equivalent to that episode.
source_text: Do not give your soul to a woman so that she steps upon your strength.

target_units.text: Delilah said to him, “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not with me? This is the third time you have deceived me and have not told me where your great strength lies.”
She wore him down with her words all night and troubled him until he grew weary to the point of death.

He told her everything from his heart and said to her, “No razor shall come upon my head, for I am a Nazirite of God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will depart from me; I will become weak and be like everyone else.”

Delilah saw that he had told her everything from his heart. She sent and called all the foreigners’ satraps, saying, “Come up this time, for he has told me all his heart.” All the foreigners’ satrapies came up to her, bringing the silver in their hands.
She put him to sleep between her knees, called the barber, and had the seven curls of his head shaved. He began to be humbled, and his strength departed from him.

Delilah said to him, “The foreigners are upon you, Samson!” He awoke from his sleep and said, “I will go out as at other times and shake myself free.” But he did not know that the Lord had departed from him.
The foreigners seized him and dug out his eyes. They brought him down to Gaza, bound him with bronze fetters, and he ground grain in the prison house.

relationship: close seduction and trap warning
rationale: Sirach warns against a courtesan's traps; Proverbs describes seductive conversation leading a young man like a bird into a trap.
source_text: Do not encounter a woman who acts as a courtesan, lest you fall into her traps.

target_units.text: She led him astray with much conversation and drove him off course with snares from her lips.
He followed her, made a fool, as an ox is led to slaughter and as a dog to bonds,
or as a deer struck in the liver by an arrow. He hurries like a bird into a trap, not knowing that he runs for his life.

relationship: close restraint of attention toward a virgin
rationale: Sirach forbids closely studying a virgin; Job likewise binds his eyes not to direct attention toward a virgin.
source_text: Do not study a virgin closely, lest you stumble into penalties on her account.

target_units.text: “I established a covenant for my eyes, and I will not direct my attention toward a virgin.

relationship: close prostitution and lost wealth warning
rationale: Sirach links giving oneself to prostitutes with losing an inheritance; Proverbs similarly says tending prostitutes destroys wealth.
source_text: Do not give your soul to prostitutes, so that you do not lose your inheritance.

target_units.text: When a man loves wisdom, his father rejoices; but one who tends prostitutes will destroy wealth.

relationship: narrative background for dangerous wandering
rationale: Sirach warns against roaming city streets and deserted places; Proverbs places the senseless young man near the woman's passageways and depicts her waiting at city corners, without making every urban journey sinful.
source_text: Do not look around in the streets of a city, or wander in its deserted places.

target_units.text: passing by a corner in the passages of her houses
and talking in evening darkness, when night is still and murky,
the woman meets him, with a prostitute’s appearance, making young men’s hearts fly away.
She is fluttering with excitement and dissolute; her feet do not rest in the house.
For at one time she roams outside, and at another she lies in wait in the squares, at every corner.

relationship: close beauty, eyes and burning desire imagery
rationale: Sirach joins the captivated eye and another's beauty with affection kindled like fire; Proverbs similarly joins desire for beauty and capture by the eyes with the danger of fire in one's bosom.
source_text: Turn your eye away from a shapely woman, and do not study another’s beauty closely. Many have been led astray by a woman’s beauty, and from it affection is kindled like fire.

target_units.text: Do not let desire for beauty overcome you; do not be hunted by your own eyes, nor seized by her eyelids.
For a prostitute’s price is as much as one loaf, but a woman hunts men’s precious lives.
Will someone bind fire in his bosom without burning his garments?
Or will someone walk on fiery coals without burning his feet?

relationship: parallel danger of involvement with a married woman
rationale: Sirach warns that intimate company with a married woman can end in destruction; Proverbs likewise says going to a married woman brings guilt and the adulterer destroys his own life. The wine feast is Sirach's particular setting.
source_text: Do not sit at all with a married woman or share a wine feast with her, lest your soul turn toward her and you slip in your spirit into destruction.

target_units.text: So is the one who goes in to a married woman: he will not be acquitted, nor will anyone touching her.
It is no wonder if someone is caught stealing, for he steals to fill his appetite when hungry.
But if caught, he will repay sevenfold, and by giving all his possessions he will rescue himself.
But the adulterer, through lack of sense, brings destruction upon his own life;

relationship: close preservation of an established friendship
rationale: Sirach says not to abandon an old friend; Proverbs likewise commands preservation of one's friend and ancestral friend, without using Sirach's aged-wine comparison.
source_text: Do not abandon an old friend, for a recent one is not his equal. A new friend is new wine; when it has aged, you will drink it with gladness.

target_units.text: Do not abandon your friend or an ancestral friend, and do not enter your brother’s house when misfortune strikes you; a nearby friend is better than a brother dwelling far away.

relationship: close prohibition of envying sinners
rationale: Both forbid envy of sinners and turn attention beyond their present appearance: Sirach to an unknown downfall and Proverbs to enduring hope under fear of the Lord.
source_text: Do not envy a sinner’s glory, for you do not know what his downfall will be.

target_units.text: Do not let your heart envy sinners, but be in the fear of the Lord the whole day;
for if you keep these things, you will have offspring, and your hope will not depart.

relationship: parallel reversal of the ungodly's apparent prosperity
rationale: Sirach rejects pleasure in ungodly prosperity because judgment remains; the psalm's account of envied sinners reaches their sudden desolation when their end is understood.
source_text: Do not take pleasure in the prosperity of the ungodly; remember that even down to Hades they will certainly not be acquitted.

target_units.text: until I enter God’s sanctuary and understand their last things.
Nevertheless, because of their deceits Thou didst set things for them; Thou didst cast them down when they were lifted up.
How they became desolate suddenly! They failed; they perished through their lawlessness.

relationship: close warning against provoking deadly royal authority
rationale: Sirach counsels caution near a person empowered to kill; Proverbs likewise compares a king's threat to a lion's wrath and says provoking him endangers one's life.
source_text: Keep far away from a person who has authority to kill, and you will certainly not suspect the fear of death. If you do approach him, do not offend, so that he does not take away your life. Recognize that you are crossing among traps and walking upon a city’s battlements.

target_units.text: A king’s threat does not differ at all from a lion’s wrath, and one who provokes him sins against his own life.

relationship: parallel counsel to seek wise company
rationale: Sirach urges counsel with the wise; Proverbs likewise connects walking with wise people with becoming wise.
source_text: To the best of your strength, take the measure of your neighbors, and seek counsel with the wise.

target_units.text: One who walks with the wise will be wise, but one who walks with fools will be known.

relationship: parallel habitual discourse in divine instruction
rationale: Sirach makes the Most High's law the content of discourse; Deuteronomy likewise places God's commands in the heart and in conversation throughout ordinary life.
source_text: Let your deliberation be with people of understanding, and let all your discourse be in the law of the Most High.

target_units.text: And these words, which I command you this day, shall be in your heart and in your soul.
And you shall teach them to your sons, and speak of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk in the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

relationship: close righteous table-company principle
rationale: Sirach chooses righteous table companions; the psalm similarly refuses to eat with the proud and looks to the land's faithful as those who may sit with the speaker.
source_text: Let righteous men be your table companions, and let your boast be in the fear of the Lord.

target_units.text: The one secretly speaking against his neighbor I used to drive away; with a proud eye and an insatiable heart, with that one I did not eat.
My eyes were on the faithful of the land, that they might sit with me; the one walking in a blameless way used to minister to me.

relationship: related wisdom manifested through speech
rationale: Sirach says a people's leader is wise through his speech; Ecclesiastes likewise distinguishes the gracious words of the wise from a fool's destructive lips. The craftsmanship comparison remains Sirach's own.
source_text: A work will be praised through the hand of craftsmen, and a leader of the people is wise through his speech.

target_units.text: The words of a wise person’s mouth are gracious, but a fool’s lips will drown him.

relationship: parallel danger of rash foolish speech
rationale: Sirach describes fear and hatred produced by talkative rashness; Proverbs likewise makes the rash mouth a source of evils and personal ruin, without specifying the same civic reaction.
source_text: A talkative man is feared in his city, and one who is rash in his speech will be hated.

target_units.text: A fool’s lips lead him into evils, and his rash mouth calls upon death.
A fool’s mouth is ruin for him, and his lips are a trap for his life.

relationship: narrative example of discerning government
rationale: Sirach links wise judgment with an instructed, orderly people; Israel's response to Solomon's judgment recognizes divine discernment enabling him to do justice.
source_text: A wise judge will instruct his people, and the government of an understanding person will be orderly.

target_units.text: All Israel heard this judgment the king had given, and they feared the king, for they saw that God’s discernment was within him to carry out justice.

relationship: close ruler and subordinate conduct relationship
rationale: Sirach connects the ruler's character with that of ministers and inhabitants; Proverbs specifically says a king's attention to unjust speech makes those under him lawless.
source_text: As the judge of a people is, so are his ministers; as the ruler of a city is, so are all who inhabit it.

target_units.text: When a king listens to an unjust word, all those under him are lawless.

relationship: parallel ruler's effect on a country's stability
rationale: Sirach contrasts destructive ignorance with rulers' understanding that settles a city; Proverbs likewise contrasts the righteous king who raises a country with the lawless person who tears it down.
source_text: An uninstructed king will destroy his people, but a city will be settled through the understanding of its rulers.

target_units.text: A righteous king raises up a country, but a lawless man tears it down.

relationship: close divine appointment and removal of rulers
rationale: Sirach places earthly authority and the raising of a fitting ruler in God's hand; Daniel likewise says God transfers and appoints kings as He changes times.
source_text: Authority over the earth is in the Lord’s hand, and at the right time He will raise up the fitting person over it.

target_units.text: He changes seasons and times, transfers kings and appoints them, gives wisdom to the wise and understanding to those who possess knowledge,

relationship: related human achievement in God's hand
rationale: Sirach places a person's prosperity in the Lord's hand; Ecclesiastes likewise places the righteous, wise and their works in God's hand. It does not repeat the specific glory given to a scribe.
source_text: A man’s prosperity is in the Lord’s hand, and He will place His glory upon the face of a scribe.

target_units.text: For I set all this upon my heart, and my heart saw all this: the righteous, the wise and their works are in God’s hand. A person knows neither love nor hatred; everything lies before them.

relationship: close prohibition of retained anger against a neighbor
rationale: Sirach warns against bearing anger over wrongs; Leviticus likewise forbids hatred, vengeance and remaining angry with one's people while commanding neighbor-love.
source_text: Do not bear anger toward your neighbor over every wrong, and do nothing by acts of insolence.

target_units.text: You shall not hate your brother in your mind; you shall surely reprove your neighbour, and you shall not bear sin because of him.
And your hand shall not take vengeance, neither shall you remain angry with the sons of your people; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself; I am the Lord.

relationship: parallel divine rejection of pride
rationale: Sirach calls pride hateful before God and people; Proverbs likewise calls the high-hearted person unclean before God, without expressly repeating human disapproval.
source_text: Pride is hateful before the Lord and human beings, and injustice is offensive to both.

target_units.text: Everyone high of heart is unclean before God, and one who unjustly puts hands into a hand will not be acquitted.

relationship: related displacement of nations for wrongdoing
rationale: Sirach explains transferred sovereignty through wrongdoing; Wisdom describes the removal of the land's ancient inhabitants for detestable practices and its settlement by God's children. The references to money and political transfer are not identical.
source_text: Sovereignty passes from nation to nation because of injustices, acts of insolence, and money.

target_units.text: For the ancient inhabitants of Thy holy land,
whom Thou didst hate for practicing the most detestable things— works of sorcery and unholy rites,
merciless murders of children, and an entrail-devouring feast of human flesh and blood— initiates from the midst of a ritual company,
and parents who were murderers of helpless lives, Thou didst will to destroy by the hands of our fathers,
so that the land most precious to Thee of all might receive a worthy settlement of God’s children.

relationship: close earth-and-ashes language in a humility setting
rationale: Sirach questions pride in earth and ashes; Abraham calls himself earth and ashes when cautiously addressing the Lord. This comparison concerns that shared humility image, not Sirach's difficult entrails clause.
source_text: Why are earth and ashes proud? For even in life I have cast out his entrails.

target_units.text: And Abraham answered and said, “Now I have begun to speak to the Lord, though I am earth and ashes.

relationship: parallel mortality of rulers
rationale: Sirach contrasts kingship today with death tomorrow; the psalm warns against trust in rulers whose spirit departs and plans perish. The physician's mockery in Sirach is not supplied by the psalm.
source_text: A long illness—the physician mocks it. A king today, and tomorrow he will die.

target_units.text: Do not trust in rulers and in sons of men who have no salvation.
His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their reasonings will perish.

relationship: close death and worm imagery
rationale: Sirach says the dead inherit creeping things and worms; Isaiah depicts fallen royal glory in Hades with decay beneath and a worm as covering.
source_text: For when a person dies, he will inherit creeping things, beasts, and worms.

target_units.text: Your glory went down to Hades, your abundant gladness. They will spread decay beneath you, and your covering is a worm.

relationship: close pride joined to departure from God
rationale: Sirach makes withdrawal from the Maker the beginning of pride; Deuteronomy likewise warns that a lifted-up heart can forget the Lord amid prosperity.
source_text: The beginning of a person’s pride is to withdraw from the Lord; his heart has departed from his Maker.

target_units.text: Take heed unto yourself, lest you forget the Lord your God, and fail to keep His commandments, and His judgments, and His ordinances which I command you this day;
lest, when you have eaten and are filled, and have built good houses and dwelt in them,
and your herds and your flocks are multiplied, and your silver and your gold are multiplied, and all that you have is multiplied,
you become lifted up in heart, and forget the Lord your God, who brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage;

relationship: parallel arrogant wrongdoing followed by collapse
rationale: Sirach joins pride and abomination with divine overthrow; Proverbs likewise places insolence before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall.
source_text: For the beginning of pride is sin, and the one who holds it fast will rain down abomination. Therefore the Lord made the calamities extraordinary and overthrew them completely.

target_units.text: Insolence leads before ruin, and evil-mindedness before a fall.

relationship: close throne reversal and elevation of the lowly
rationale: Sirach describes the Lord pulling down rulers' thrones and seating the gentle; Mary's song likewise joins scattered pride with rulers brought down from thrones and the lowly raised.
source_text: The Lord pulled down the thrones of rulers and seated the gentle in their place.

target_units.text: He has performed a mighty deed with His arm; He scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.
He brought rulers down from thrones and raised up the lowly.

relationship: close displaced nations and planted successors imagery
rationale: Sirach contrasts uprooted nations with planted humble people; the psalm likewise says God destroyed nations and planted the fathers, without explicitly naming those fathers humble in that verse.
source_text: The Lord plucked out the roots of nations and planted the humble in their place.

target_units.text: Thy hand destroyed nations, and Thou didst plant our fathers; Thou didst afflict peoples and cast them out.

relationship: parallel divine destruction of nations and cities
rationale: Sirach describes national lands overthrown to their foundations; the psalm likewise describes rebuked nations and cities pulled down, without repeating the foundation image.
source_text: The Lord overthrew the lands of nations and destroyed them down to the foundations of the earth.

target_units.text: Thou didst rebuke nations, and the ungodly one perished; Thou didst erase their name for ever and for the age of the age.
The enemy’s swords failed utterly, and Thou didst pull down cities; their memory perished with a noise.

relationship: close destruction and erased memory motif
rationale: Sirach joins destruction with memory ceasing from earth; the psalm likewise joins perished nations with erased names and vanished memory.
source_text: He removed some from among them and destroyed them, and made their memory cease from the earth.

target_units.text: Thou didst rebuke nations, and the ungodly one perished; Thou didst erase their name for ever and for the age of the age.
The enemy’s swords failed utterly, and Thou didst pull down cities; their memory perished with a noise.

relationship: parallel honor determined by fear of the Lord
rationale: Sirach distinguishes honorable God-fearing people from commandment-breakers; the psalm similarly contrasts contempt for wickedness with honor for those fearing the Lord.
source_text: What offspring is honorable? Human offspring. What offspring is honorable? Those who fear the Lord. What offspring is dishonorable? Human offspring. What offspring is dishonorable? Those who transgress commandments.

target_units.text: One who acts wickedly is held in contempt before him, but he honors those who fear the Lord; one who swears to his neighbor and does not set it aside.

relationship: close honoring those who fear God
rationale: Sirach identifies those fearing the Lord as honored in His eyes; the psalm makes honoring such people a mark of the faithful worshiper, alongside contempt for wicked conduct.
source_text: Among brothers their leader is honored, and those who fear the Lord are honored in His eyes.

target_units.text: One who acts wickedly is held in contempt before him, but he honors those who fear the Lord; one who swears to his neighbor and does not set it aside.

relationship: parallel God-directed boasting above wealth or standing
rationale: Sirach gives rich, renowned and poor the same boast in fear of the Lord; Jeremiah rejects boasting in wealth, strength or wisdom and directs it toward understanding and knowing the Lord.
source_text: Rich, renowned, and poor alike—their boast is the fear of the Lord.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Let no wise man boast in his wisdom, let no strong man boast in his strength, and let no rich man boast in his wealth,
but let whoever boasts boast in this: understanding and knowing that I am the Lord, doing mercy and judgment and righteousness upon the earth, because in these is My will, says the Lord.

relationship: warning and example concerning despised poor wisdom
rationale: Sirach says it is wrong to dishonor an understanding poor person; Ecclesiastes describes the corresponding injustice of a poor man's saving wisdom being forgotten and despised.
source_text: It is not right to dishonor an understanding poor person, and it is not fitting to glorify a sinful man.

target_units.text: and he might find in it a poor wise man, who will deliver the city by his wisdom; yet no one remembered that poor man.
I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.

relationship: related divine regard beyond human distinctions
rationale: Sirach denies that recognized officeholders are greater than the person who fears the Lord; Peter similarly grounds divine acceptance in fear and righteous conduct rather than partiality, without reproducing the same ranking of offices.
source_text: A dignitary, judge, and ruler will be glorified, but none of them is greater than the one who fears the Lord.

target_units.text: Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality,
but in every nation, whoever fears Him and practices righteousness is acceptable to Him.

relationship: close wise servant ruling social superiors
rationale: Sirach says free people will serve a wise household slave; Proverbs likewise says an intelligent household servant will rule foolish masters.
source_text: Free people will serve a wise household slave, and a knowledgeable man will not grumble.

target_units.text: An intelligent household servant will rule foolish masters, and divide portions among brothers.

relationship: close useful work contrasted with hungry pretension
rationale: Sirach prefers a working person with enough to one displaying glory without bread; Proverbs likewise prefers the dishonored person who serves himself to one clothed in honor but needing bread.
source_text: Better someone who works and has abundance in everything than someone who walks about enjoying glory but lacks bread.

target_units.text: Better is a man in dishonor who serves himself than one who clothes himself in honor but needs bread.

relationship: parallel inward honor expressed in gentleness
rationale: Sirach urges giving the soul honor with gentleness; Peter likewise identifies the hidden heart's gentle spirit as imperishable beauty precious before God.
source_text: Child, glorify your soul with gentleness, and give it honor according to its worth.

target_units.text: but the hidden person of the heart, in the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious before God.

relationship: related moral injury against one's own life
rationale: Sirach questions justification or honor for one harming his own soul; Proverbs similarly describes rejecting discipline as hatred of oneself and accepting rebuke as love for one's life.
source_text: Who will justify the one who sins against his own soul? Who will glorify the one who dishonors his own life?

target_units.text: One who thrusts discipline away hates himself, but one who keeps rebukes loves his own life.

relationship: contrast in the recognition of poor wisdom
rationale: Sirach names knowledge as a poor person's ground for honor; Ecclesiastes observes that the poor man's wisdom is nevertheless despised, exposing the social failure to give that honor.
source_text: A poor person is glorified for his knowledge, and a rich person is glorified for his wealth.

target_units.text: I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.

relationship: close elevation of the lowly to seats with rulers
rationale: Sirach says humble wisdom raises a person's head to sit among dignitaries; Hannah's song likewise describes God lifting the poor to sit with rulers, without naming wisdom as the means.
source_text: The wisdom of a humble person will raise his head and seat him among dignitaries.

target_units.text: He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to seat them with rulers of peoples and grant them a throne of glory as their inheritance,

relationship: close rejection of judgment by appearance
rationale: Sirach forbids praise or contempt based on appearance; God likewise tells Samuel not to judge by appearance or height, contrasting the face with the heart.
source_text: Do not praise a man for his beauty or loathe a person for his appearance.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Samuel, “Do not look at his appearance or the bearing of his height, for I have treated him as nothing. God does not see as a human looks: a human looks at the face, but God looks at the heart.”

relationship: close esteem for the small but productive bee
rationale: Sirach contrasts the bee's small size with her excellent sweet product; Proverbs likewise praises her useful, esteemed labor despite bodily weakness.
source_text: The bee is small among winged creatures, but her product is foremost among sweet things.

target_units.text: Or go to the bee and learn how industrious she is, and how nobly she performs her work,
whose labors kings and private people use for health; she is desired by everyone and held in esteem.
Although weak in bodily strength, she was advanced because she honored wisdom.

relationship: parallel restraint of outward adornment's importance
rationale: Sirach warns against boasting in clothing; Peter likewise shifts valued adornment from garments and ornaments to the hidden heart's gentle spirit, without repeating Sirach's account of hidden divine works.
source_text: Do not boast in the clothing you wear or exalt yourself on a day of glory. For the Lord’s works are wonderful, and His works are hidden from human beings.

target_units.text: Let your adornment not be the outward kind—braiding hair, putting on gold ornaments, or dressing in garments—
but the hidden person of the heart, in the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious before God.

relationship: parallel reversal of ruling status
rationale: Sirach describes rulers on the ground and an unexpected wearer of a crown; Mary's song likewise contrasts rulers brought down from thrones with lowly people raised up.
source_text: Many rulers have sat upon the ground, while someone unsuspected wore a diadem.

target_units.text: He brought rulers down from thrones and raised up the lowly.

relationship: related humbling of the powerful
rationale: Sirach recalls powerful and renowned people dishonored and handed over; Mary's song likewise describes proud people scattered and rulers brought down, without naming the same captors.
source_text: Many powerful people have been greatly dishonored, and the renowned were handed into others’ hands.

target_units.text: He has performed a mighty deed with His arm; He scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.
He brought rulers down from thrones and raised up the lowly.

relationship: close investigation before judgment
rationale: Sirach requires investigation and understanding before rebuke; Nicodemus likewise asks whether the Law judges before hearing a person and knowing the facts.
source_text: Do not find fault before investigating; understand first, and then rebuke.

target_units.text: Nicodemus, who had come to Him earlier and was one of them, said to them,
“Does our Law judge a person unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?”

relationship: close hearing before answering
rationale: Both reject answering before hearing; Sirach also expressly prohibits interrupting another person's words.
source_text: Do not answer before hearing, and do not interrupt in the middle of someone’s words.

target_units.text: One who answers a word before hearing it—it is foolishness and reproach for him.

relationship: close warning against another person's dispute
rationale: Sirach warns against quarrels that do not concern oneself; Proverbs likewise compares presiding over another's dispute with grasping a dog's tail.
source_text: Do not quarrel about a matter that is no concern of yours, and do not sit together in the judgment of sinners.

target_units.text: As one who grasps a dog’s tail, so is one who presides over another’s dispute.

relationship: related restraint of excessive toil
rationale: Sirach warns that multiplying activities cannot secure escape from blame or frustration; Ecclesiastes similarly prefers a handful of rest to two handfuls of toil, without stating the same pursuit-and-flight paradox.
source_text: Child, do not let your activities concern too many things. If you multiply them, you will not escape blame; even if you pursue, you will certainly not catch up, and even by running away you will certainly not escape.

target_units.text: Better a handful of rest than two handfuls of toil and resolve of spirit.

relationship: parallel failure of strenuous toil to secure its hoped-for result
rationale: Sirach observes labor and haste ending in greater want; the psalm likewise calls early rising and painful labor vain apart from the Lord's action, providing a related theological account of frustrated effort.
source_text: There is someone who toils, labors, and hurries, yet is all the more in want.

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. For Solomon. Unless the Lord builds a house, those building it have labored in vain. Unless the Lord guards a city, the watchman has kept awake in vain.
It is vain for you to rise early, to get up after sitting down, you who eat bread of pain, when He gives sleep to His beloved ones.

relationship: close divine lifting of the helpless poor
rationale: Sirach's weak, impoverished person is raised when the Lord looks kindly on him; Hannah's song likewise describes God lifting the poor from the earth and dung heap.
source_text: There is someone slow who needs support, lacking strength and abounding in poverty. Yet the Lord’s eyes looked upon him for good, and He raised him from his low estate

target_units.text: He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to seat them with rulers of peoples and grant them a throne of glory as their inheritance,

relationship: parallel public elevation of the lowly
rationale: The lifted head continues Sirach's account of the impoverished person's reversal; Hannah's song likewise describes the poor receiving a seat with rulers. It does not expressly report the spectators' marveling.
source_text: and lifted his head, and many marveled at him.

target_units.text: He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to seat them with rulers of peoples and grant them a throne of glory as their inheritance,

relationship: close divine authority over life, death, poverty and wealth
rationale: Sirach attributes life's opposing conditions to the Lord; Hannah's song likewise explicitly gives Him authority to kill, enliven, impoverish and enrich.
source_text: Good things and bad, life and death, poverty and wealth are from the Lord.

target_units.text: The Lord puts to death and gives life; He brings down to Hades and brings up.
The Lord makes poor and makes rich; He humbles and raises high.

relationship: parallel enduring provision for the godly
rationale: Sirach says the Lord's gift remains with the godly; the psalm likewise promises the blameless an enduring inheritance and provision in evil times.
source_text: The Lord’s gift remains with the godly, and His good pleasure will prosper for ever.

target_units.text: The Lord knows the ways of the blameless, and their inheritance will last for ever.
They will not be put to shame in an evil time, and in days of famine they will be filled.

relationship: close rich man's promised rest interrupted by death
rationale: Both portray a person promising himself rest and enjoyment of stored goods while failing to reckon with death and the goods passing beyond his control.
source_text: when he says, “I have found rest, and now I will eat from my good things,” he does not know how much time will pass before he leaves them to others and dies.

target_units.text: And I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, be glad!”’
But God said to him, ‘Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’

relationship: parallel steadfast perseverance in faithful work
rationale: Sirach counsels remaining in one's covenant and growing old in work; Paul likewise urges steadfast abundance in the Lord's work, grounding it specifically in resurrection hope.
source_text: Stand firm in your covenant, occupy yourself with it, and grow old in your work.

target_units.text: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, knowing that your labor is not empty in the Lord.

relationship: close trust and perseverance instead of envy at sinners
rationale: Sirach rejects amazement at sinners' success while counseling trust and labor; the psalm likewise joins hope in the Lord and good action with refusal to envy the prospering lawless.
source_text: Do not marvel at a sinner’s works, but trust the Lord and remain at your labor. For it is easy in the Lord’s eyes to make a poor person rich quickly and suddenly.

target_units.text: Hope in the Lord and show kindness; settle in the land, and you will be pastured on its wealth.
Delight yourself in the Lord, and He will give you the requests of your heart.
Reveal your way to the Lord; hope in Him, and He will act.
He will bring out your righteousness like light, and your judgment like noon.
Submit to the Lord and beseech Him; do not be provoked to envy by one prospering in his way, by a person committing lawless deeds.

relationship: close blessing as the source of righteous prosperity
rationale: Sirach attributes the godly person's flourishing reward to the Lord's blessing; Proverbs likewise says that His blessing rests upon the righteous and makes rich.
source_text: The Lord’s blessing is in the godly person’s reward, and in a swift moment He makes His blessing flourish.

target_units.text: The Lord’s blessing is upon the head of the righteous; it makes rich, and sorrow in the heart will certainly not be added to it.

relationship: close presumptuous denial of future adversity
rationale: Sirach forbids saying that sufficient possessions exclude future harm; the psalm depicts a sinner similarly declaring that he will remain unshaken and without adversity.
source_text: Do not say, “I have enough; what harm can come to me from now on?”

target_units.text: For he said in his heart, “I will certainly not be shaken, from generation to generation, without adversity.”

relationship: related counsel concerning alternating good and bad days
rationale: Sirach observes that each kind of day drives out memory of the other; Ecclesiastes likewise pairs days of goodness and evil, urging consideration of God's arrangement rather than assuming present conditions exhaust reality.
source_text: On a day of good things, bad things are forgotten; on a day of bad things, good things will not be remembered.

target_units.text: On a day of goodness, live in good; on a day of evil, consider: God has made this in accord with that concerning speech, so that human beings may find out nothing that comes after them.

relationship: close repayment according to deeds
rationale: Sirach places repayment according to one's ways at death; Romans likewise announces divine repayment according to works, within its description of the day of righteous judgment.
source_text: For it is easy before the Lord, on the day of death, to repay a person according to his ways.

target_units.text: who will repay each according to his works:
to those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory and honor and incorruptibility, eternal life;
but to those acting from selfish ambition, who disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, wrath and fury,

relationship: related assessment of life in view of its end
rationale: Sirach postpones calling a person happy until death; Ecclesiastes likewise gives the day of death priority over birth and makes life's end instructive. The statement about knowing a man through his children is not repeated there.
source_text: Call no one happy before his death, and a man will be known in his children.

target_units.text: A name is better than good oil, and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.
Better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of drinking, for this is the end of every human being, and the living will take it to heart.

relationship: parallel exclusion of deceptive house companions
rationale: Sirach warns against receiving everyone into one's house because of deceitful ambushes; the psalm likewise excludes arrogance from the house and unjust speech from the speaker's presence.
source_text: Do not bring every person into your house, for the deceitful person has many ambushes.

target_units.text: One practicing arrogance did not dwell within my house; one speaking unjust things did not prosper before my eyes.

relationship: related concealed watching for another's fall
rationale: Sirach likens a proud person's heart to a decoy and watching spy; the psalm likewise describes hostile people concealing themselves and watching the speaker's heel, without using the partridge image.
source_text: Like a decoy partridge in a basket is the heart of a proud person; like a spy, he watches for a fall.

target_units.text: All day they detested my words; all their thoughts against me are for evil.
They will sojourn and conceal themselves; they will watch my heel, just as they waited for my soul.

relationship: close moral inversion of good and evil
rationale: Sirach describes an ambusher turning good things into bad and blaming what is choice; Isaiah likewise condemns calling good evil and evil good, without specifying the same ambush.
source_text: For he lies in wait, turning good things into bad, and will attach blame to what is choice.

target_units.text: Woe to those calling evil good and good evil, making darkness light and light darkness, making bitter sweet and sweet bitter!

relationship: close small-fire image applied to growing evil
rationale: Sirach joins a spark growing into coals with a sinner's ambush for blood; James likewise uses a small fire spreading widely to describe the destructive tongue. The particular forms of wrongdoing differ.
source_text: From a spark of fire a bed of coals grows, and a sinful person lies in ambush for blood.

target_units.text: So also the tongue is a small member and boasts great things. Look how small a fire sets so great a forest ablaze!
And the tongue is a fire. The tongue is established among our members as a world of unrighteousness, staining the whole body, setting the wheel of life ablaze, and itself set ablaze by Gehenna.

relationship: parallel caution against planned evil
rationale: Sirach warns against an evildoer's plans and lasting blame; Proverbs likewise counsels distance from people planning bloodshed and explains the ruin entailed by their paths.
source_text: Beware of an evildoer, for he devises evil, lest he give you lasting blame.

target_units.text: Son, do not let ungodly men lead you astray; do not agree if they invite you, saying,
Come with us; share in bloodshed. Let us hide a righteous man in the earth unjustly;
let us swallow him alive like Hades and remove his memory from the earth.
Let us seize his costly property and fill our houses with spoils.
Cast your lot among us; let us all obtain a common purse, and let there be one moneybag for us.
Do not walk in the way with them; turn your foot away from their paths,
for their feet run toward evil, and they are quick to shed blood.
For nets are not unjustly stretched out for winged creatures.
For those who share in murder store up evils for themselves, and the overthrow of lawless men is evil.
These are the ways of all who carry out lawless deeds, for through ungodliness they take away their own life.

relationship: parallel reward for receiving the righteous
rationale: Sirach promises repayment from the godly recipient or the Most High; Jesus likewise promises reward for receiving a righteous person or giving even a cup of water in a disciple's name.
source_text: Do good to a godly person, and you will find repayment; if not from him, then from the Most High.

target_units.text: Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.
And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, will certainly not lose his reward.”

relationship: parallel loss of help through refusal of charity
rationale: Sirach denies good things to one withholding alms; Proverbs likewise says one who refuses to hear the weak will call without receiving a hearing. Sirach also includes persistence in evil.
source_text: There will be no good things for the one who persists in evil and the one who gives no alms.

target_units.text: One who blocks his ears from hearing the weak will himself also call, and there will be no one listening.

relationship: contrast over doing good to sinners
rationale: Sirach limits support to the godly and forbids supporting a sinner; Jesus commands good toward enemies and describes the Most High as kind to the ungrateful and evil. The different directions are preserved.
source_text: Give to the godly person, and do not support the sinner.

target_units.text: But love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing back. Your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, because He is kind to the ungrateful and evil.

relationship: contrast over feeding a dangerous adversary
rationale: Sirach counsels withholding loaves from the ungodly to avoid being overpowered; Paul instead commands feeding a hungry enemy and overcoming evil with good, rather than presenting the two instructions as identical.
source_text: Do good to the humble person, and do not give to the ungodly. Hold back his loaves and do not give them to him, so that he does not use them to overpower you. For you will receive double evils for all the good things you do to him.

target_units.text: But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head.
Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.

relationship: close divine hatred and judgment of wrongdoing
rationale: Sirach grounds retribution in the Most High's hatred of sinners; the psalm likewise joins hatred of lawlessness's practitioners with destruction of falsehood and abhorrence of bloodshed and deceit.
source_text: For the Most High Himself has hated sinners and will repay the ungodly with retribution.

target_units.text: The lawless will not remain before Thine eyes; Thou didst hate all who work lawlessness.
Thou wilt destroy all who speak falsehood; the Lord abhors a man of bloodshed and deceit.

relationship: contrast in the extent of benevolence
rationale: Sirach says to give to the good and not support the sinner; Paul gives special attention to the household of faith while expressly extending good to everyone.
source_text: Give to the good person, and do not support the sinner.

target_units.text: So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, especially to those of the household of faith.

relationship: related testing of friendship in adversity
rationale: Sirach says prosperity does not vindicate a friend and adversity exposes an enemy; Proverbs calls for a friend at all times and brothers useful in need, stating the fidelity such testing seeks.
source_text: A friend will not be vindicated in prosperity, and an enemy will not remain hidden in adversity.

target_units.text: Let a friend be yours at all times, and let brothers be useful in times of need; for this is why they are born.

relationship: close poverty and abandoned friendship observation
rationale: Sirach observes that even a friend separates in adversity; Proverbs similarly contrasts wealth's many friends with the poor person abandoned by his existing friend.
source_text: When a man prospers, his enemies are in grief; when he suffers adversity, even his friend will separate himself.

target_units.text: Wealth adds many friends, but the poor person is abandoned even by the friend he has.

relationship: parallel distrust of concealed enmity
rationale: Sirach compares an enemy's wickedness with copper's corrosion; Proverbs likewise exposes deceptive lips concealing hostility, without the corrosion comparison.
source_text: Never trust your enemy, for as copper corrodes, so does his wickedness.

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;
if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.
One who hides enmity establishes deceit, but one well known in councils discloses his own sins.

relationship: parallel suspicion of an enemy's conciliatory behavior
rationale: Sirach warns against trusting bowed, apparently humble behavior; Proverbs likewise says not to be persuaded by an enemy's tearful entreaty because hidden evil remains. The wiped-mirror image is not repeated.
source_text: Even if he humbles himself and walks bowed down, keep your soul alert and guard against him. You will be toward him like someone who has wiped a mirror, and you will know that it has not completely corroded.

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;
if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.

relationship: close snake-charmer and snakebite image
rationale: Sirach asks who would pity a charmer bitten by a serpent; Ecclesiastes likewise describes a snake biting without a charm and no advantage for the charmer, without posing the same question about pity.
source_text: Who will pity a snake-charmer bitten by a serpent, or all those who approach wild beasts?

target_units.text: If the snake bites without a whispered charm, there is no advantage for the charmer.

relationship: parallel danger of joining sinful companions
rationale: Sirach warns that approaching a sinner entangles one in his sins; Proverbs likewise commands distance from lawless companions' paths and describes their destructive outcome.
source_text: So it is with the one who approaches a sinful man and becomes entangled in his sins.

target_units.text: Do not walk in the way with them; turn your foot away from their paths,
for their feet run toward evil, and they are quick to shed blood.
For nets are not unjustly stretched out for winged creatures.
For those who share in murder store up evils for themselves, and the overthrow of lawless men is evil.
These are the ways of all who carry out lawless deeds, for through ungodliness they take away their own life.

relationship: related instability of conditional friendship
rationale: Sirach describes an associate who stays briefly but does not hold firm if the addressee turns aside; Proverbs describes abandonment in poverty, a different stated condition for failed loyalty.
source_text: He will stay with you for an hour, but if you turn aside, he will certainly not hold firm.

target_units.text: Wealth adds many friends, but the poor person is abandoned even by the friend he has.

relationship: close weeping lips concealing hostile plans
rationale: Both depict an enemy whose agreeable, tearful outward speech masks deception in his heart; Sirach additionally specifies a pit and appetite for blood.
source_text: An enemy will make his lips sweet, but in his heart he will plan to throw you into a pit. An enemy will weep with his eyes, but if he finds the occasion, he will not be satisfied with blood.

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;
if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.
One who hides enmity establishes deceit, but one well known in councils discloses his own sins.

relationship: related betrayal beneath an appearance of help
rationale: Sirach depicts an enemy posing as a helper while undermining one's heel; the psalm joins whispered hostile plans with treachery by a trusted table companion, without repeating the helper's pretense verbatim.
source_text: If evil things meet you, you will find him there before you; as though helping, he will undermine your heel.

target_units.text: Together all my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evils for me.
They laid a lawless word against me: “Can it be that the one lying down will not rise again?”
For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my loaves, magnified treachery against me.

relationship: close hostile clapping and head-shaking gestures
rationale: Sirach describes the enemy shaking his head and clapping; Lamentations likewise depicts onlookers clapping and shaking their heads at fallen Jerusalem alongside hostile speech.
source_text: He will shake his head and clap his hands, whisper many things, and change his expression.

target_units.text: All who pass along the road clapped their hands at you. They hissed and shook their heads at Daughter Jerusalem: “Is this the city they will call a crown of glory, the gladness of all the earth?”
All your enemies opened their mouths against you. They hissed and gnashed their teeth; they said, “We have swallowed her! Indeed, this is the day we expected; we found it, we saw it!”

relationship: parallel harmful conduct learned through association
rationale: Sirach says association with the proud makes a person like them; Proverbs similarly warns that companionship with an angry person teaches his ways, using a different harmful disposition.
source_text: The one who touches pitch will be stained, and the one who associates with a proud person will become like him.

target_units.text: Do not be a companion to a quick-tempered man, and do not lodge with an angry friend,
lest you learn his ways and take nooses for your own life.

relationship: close warning against a poor person's attempt to match the rich
rationale: Sirach warns against burdens beyond one's strength and unequal association with the wealthy; Proverbs likewise tells a poor person not to stretch himself to match a rich man. The pottery collision is Sirach's distinct image.
source_text: Do not lift a burden beyond you, and do not associate with someone stronger and richer than you. What fellowship can an earthen pot have with a cauldron? One will strike, and the other will be shattered.

target_units.text: Do not stretch yourself, being poor, to match a rich man, but hold back in your own reflection;
If you fix your eye upon him, he will appear nowhere, for wings like an eagle’s have been prepared for him, and he returns to the house of the one who presides over him.

relationship: parallel coercion by the wealthy against the poor
rationale: Sirach contrasts a rich wrongdoer's threats with the injured poor person's entreaties; James likewise calls the rich oppressors who drag others into courts, without describing the same entreaties.
source_text: A rich person has done wrong, yet he has added threats; a poor person has been wronged, yet he will add entreaties.

target_units.text: But you have dishonored the poor person. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into courts?

relationship: close wealth-dependent companionship
rationale: Sirach's wealthy associate uses someone useful but abandons one in need; Proverbs likewise contrasts wealth's many friends with abandonment in poverty.
source_text: If you are useful, he makes use of you; if you are in want, he will abandon you.

target_units.text: Wealth adds many friends, but the poor person is abandoned even by the friend he has.

relationship: parallel pleasant speech concealing an exploitative purpose
rationale: Sirach exposes smiles and hopeful promises used to mislead someone needed by the speaker; Proverbs likewise exposes agreeable lips and entreaties concealing deceit and enmity.
source_text: He needs you, and he will mislead you, smile at you, and give you hope. He will say pleasant things to you and ask, “What do you need?”

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;
if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.
One who hides enmity establishes deceit, but one well known in councils discloses his own sins.

relationship: parallel harmful hospitality from an ungenerous host
rationale: Sirach warns that a rich person's food can lead to humiliation and depletion; Proverbs likewise warns against the begrudging host's food and the ruin of good words, without describing repeated depletion in the same way.
source_text: He will shame you with his food until he has emptied you out twice or three times, and in the end he will mock you. After this he will see you and abandon you and shake his head at you.

target_units.text: Do not dine with a begrudging man, and do not desire his foods,
for as if someone swallowed a hair, so he eats and drinks.
Do not bring him in to yourself and eat your morsel with him, for he will vomit it and ruin your good words.

relationship: close restraint before a powerful host's invitation
rationale: Sirach advises reserve when summoned by the powerful; Proverbs similarly discourages self-placement among rulers and prefers receiving an invitation to come higher.
source_text: When a powerful person summons you, be retiring, and he will summon you all the more.

target_units.text: Do not boast before a king, and do not station yourself in the places of rulers;
for it is better for you to be told, “Come up to me,” than for him to humble you before a ruler. Say what your eyes have seen.

relationship: close avoidance of self-promotion and public displacement
rationale: Sirach warns that thrusting oneself forward leads to being pushed away; Jesus likewise counsels taking a lower place so that the host invites one higher rather than removing one in shame. Sirach's caution against excessive distance is additional.
source_text: Do not thrust yourself forward, lest you be pushed away; do not stand too far off, so that you are not forgotten.

target_units.text: “When someone invites you to a wedding feast, do not recline in the foremost place. Someone more honored than you may have been invited by him,
and the one who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give this man your place.’ Then you will begin, with shame, to occupy the last place.

But when you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he will say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have honor before all who recline at table with you.

relationship: related danger of indiscreet disclosure
rationale: Sirach warns about a merciless person who does not keep words to himself; Proverbs likewise contrasts disclosure of plans by the double-tongued with faithful concealment. It does not promise the same harm or bonds.
source_text: Merciless is the one who does not keep words to himself, and he will certainly not spare you harm and bonds.

target_units.text: A double-tongued man reveals plans in a council, but one faithful in breath conceals matters.

relationship: close incompatible-fellowship question
rationale: Sirach asks what fellowship a wolf has with a lamb and applies it to sinner and godly person; Paul likewise asks what sharing righteousness has with lawlessness and a believer with an unbeliever.
source_text: What fellowship can a wolf have with a lamb? So it is with a sinner and a godly person.

target_units.text: Do not become unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what sharing is there between righteousness and lawlessness, or what fellowship between light and darkness?
And what harmony is there between Christ and Beliar, or what portion does a believer have with an unbeliever?

relationship: related antagonism between rich and poor
rationale: Sirach questions peace between rich and poor through an animal comparison; James supplies the concrete antagonism of rich people oppressing others and taking them to court, without the hyena-and-dog image.
source_text: What peace can a hyena have with a dog? What peace can a rich person have with a poor one?

target_units.text: But you have dishonored the poor person. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into courts?

relationship: close predatory consumption image for social oppression
rationale: Sirach compares the poor as feeding grounds for the rich with wild asses as lions' prey; Micah likewise depicts rulers consuming the people's flesh, turning exploitation into a bodily feeding image.
source_text: Wild asses in the wilderness are prey for lions; so the poor are feeding grounds for the rich.

target_units.text: He will say: “Hear these things now, authorities of Jacob’s house and remaining ones of Israel’s house! Is it not for you to know justice,
you who hate good things and seek evil things, who snatch their skins from them and their flesh from their bones?”
Just as they ate the flesh of My people, flayed their skins from their bones, crushed their bones and divided them into pieces like flesh for a cauldron and meat for a cooking pot,

relationship: parallel contempt for poverty amid social pride
rationale: Sirach describes the poor as abhorrent to the rich; James exposes the corresponding favoritism that gives the well-dressed person a good seat and demeans the poor person.
source_text: Lowliness is an abomination to the proud; so a poor person is an abomination to the rich.

target_units.text: For if a man with gold rings and splendid clothing enters your gathering, and a poor person in filthy clothing also enters,
and you pay attention to the one wearing splendid clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” but say to the poor person, “You stand, or sit there beneath my footstool,”
have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?

relationship: close wealth and poverty's opposite effects on friends
rationale: Sirach contrasts friends supporting a shaken rich person with pushing a fallen poor person farther away; Proverbs likewise contrasts multiplying friends through wealth with a poor person's abandonment.
source_text: A rich person who is shaken is supported by friends; a lowly person who falls is pushed away still further by friends.

target_units.text: Wealth adds many friends, but the poor person is abandoned even by the friend he has.

relationship: related unjust vindication linked to material advantage
rationale: Sirach describes excusing a rich person's improper speech while rebuking a poor person; Isaiah condemns vindicating the ungodly for gifts and removing the righteous person's right. The social deference and explicit bribery are related but distinct mechanisms.
source_text: When a rich person stumbles, many support him. He spoke things that should not be spoken, and they justified him. A lowly person stumbled, and they added rebuke; he spoke with understanding, and no place was given him.

target_units.text: who justify the ungodly for gifts and take away the righteous person’s right!

relationship: close disregard for poor wisdom beside powerful speech
rationale: Sirach contrasts the audience's reverence for rich speech with contempt for poor speech; Ecclesiastes likewise says poor wisdom is despised and unheard, while preferring quiet wise words to rulers' shouting.
source_text: A rich person spoke, and everyone fell silent; they raised his word to the clouds. A poor person spoke, and they said, “Who is this?” If he stumbles, they will throw him down all the more.

target_units.text: I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.
The words of the wise, heard quietly, are better than the shouting of rulers in follies.

relationship: related moral qualification of wealth's benefit
rationale: Sirach calls wealth good when free of sin; Proverbs likewise denies that treasures benefit the lawless and contrasts them with rescuing righteousness. The statement about poverty in ungodly speech remains distinct.
source_text: Wealth is good when no sin accompanies it, and poverty is evil in the mouth of the ungodly.

target_units.text: Treasures will not profit lawless people, but righteousness will rescue from death.

relationship: close heart reflected in the face
rationale: Sirach says the heart changes one's face for good or evil; Proverbs likewise contrasts a flourishing face from a glad heart with a gloomy face from sorrow.
source_text: A person’s heart changes his face, whether for good or for evil.

target_units.text: When the heart rejoices, the face flourishes, but when it is in sorrows, the face grows gloomy.

relationship: related painstaking search for wise sayings
rationale: Sirach says finding proverbs requires laborious deliberation; Ecclesiastes likewise describes an ear tracing an orderly arrangement of proverbs and the search for delightful, upright words. Sirach's cheerful-face clause is separate.
source_text: A cheerful face is the trace of a heart in good circumstances, and finding proverbs requires laborious deliberations.

target_units.text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.
Ecclesiastes sought much to find words of delight and something written in uprightness, words of truth.

relationship: close commendation of avoiding a slip in speech
rationale: Sirach calls the person who has not slipped with his mouth happy; James likewise treats not stumbling in speech as a mark of a complete person, without repeating the grief-over-sins clause.
source_text: Happy is the man who has not slipped with his mouth and has not been pierced by grief over sins.

target_units.text: For we all stumble in many things. If anyone does not stumble in speech, that person is a complete man, able to bridle his whole body also.

relationship: close confidence when the inner person does not condemn
rationale: Sirach blesses the one whose soul has not condemned him; John likewise connects a heart that does not condemn with confidence before God.
source_text: Happy is the one whose soul has not condemned him and who has not fallen away from his hope.

target_units.text: Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God,

relationship: related futility of possessions not enjoyed by their owner
rationale: Sirach questions wealth's value to a miserly, grudging owner; Ecclesiastes describes possessions the owner cannot enjoy while a stranger consumes them, assigning the inability to a different cause.
source_text: Wealth is not good for a miserly man; what are possessions for a grudging person?

target_units.text: a person to whom God will give wealth, possessions and glory, so that his soul lacks nothing it desires, yet God will not empower him to eat from it, for a stranger will eat it. This is futility and a grievous sickness.

relationship: close wealth accumulated for another's enjoyment
rationale: Sirach says self-depriving accumulation lets strangers enjoy one's goods; Ecclesiastes likewise depicts a stranger enjoying the wealthy owner's possessions, without attributing that outcome specifically to self-denial.
source_text: The one who gathers by depriving his own soul gathers for others, and strangers will enjoy his good things.

target_units.text: a person to whom God will give wealth, possessions and glory, so that his soul lacks nothing it desires, yet God will not empower him to eat from it, for a stranger will eat it. This is futility and a grievous sickness.

relationship: related connection between mercy and treatment of one's own life
rationale: Sirach questions how one who is bad to himself can be good to others; Proverbs likewise links mercy with doing good to one's own life and mercilessness with bodily destruction.
source_text: To whom will the one who is bad to himself be good? He will certainly not rejoice in his possessions.

target_units.text: A merciful man does good to his own life, but the merciless destroys his own body.

relationship: close evil-eye image for withholding generosity
rationale: Sirach describes the grudging eye turning away and disregarding souls; Deuteronomy likewise warns against an evil eye toward a needy brother that gives him nothing.
source_text: Evil is the one who begrudges with his eye, turning his face away and disregarding souls.

target_units.text: Take heed unto yourself, lest there be a hidden, lawless thought in your heart, saying: The seventh year, the year of release, draws near; and your eye be evil toward your needy brother, and you give him nothing, and he cry against you unto the Lord, and there be great sin upon you.

relationship: parallel insatiable desire for possessions
rationale: Sirach says the greedy eye is never satisfied with its share; Ecclesiastes likewise says love of silver is not filled by silver and questions wealth's benefit beyond looking at it.
source_text: A greedy person’s eye is not satisfied with its portion, and evil injustice dries up the soul.

target_units.text: Whoever loves silver will not be filled with silver; and who has loved a yield in their abundance? This too is futility.
When goodness increased, those who consumed it multiplied. What strength has its possessor except to look at it with his eyes?

relationship: close begrudging bread at an inhospitable table
rationale: Sirach describes an evil eye begrudging bread and an impoverished table; Proverbs likewise warns against the begrudging man's food and the harm of sharing a meal with him.
source_text: An evil eye begrudges bread, and his own table is lacking.

target_units.text: Do not dine with a begrudging man, and do not desire his foods,
for as if someone swallowed a hair, so he eats and drinks.
Do not bring him in to yourself and eat your morsel with him, for he will vomit it and ruin your good words.

relationship: parallel worthy offering according to one's means
rationale: Sirach joins doing good from what one has with bringing worthy offerings; Deuteronomy likewise forbids appearing empty before the Lord and measures each gift by the giver's ability and blessing.
source_text: Child, do yourself good according to what you have, and bring offerings worthily to the Lord.

target_units.text: Three times in the year shall every male among you appear before the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord shall choose: in the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and in the Feast of Weeks, and in the Feast of the Pitching of Tents. You shall not appear before the Lord your God empty,
but every man according to the ability of your hands, according to the blessing of the Lord your God which He has given you.

relationship: parallel uncertainty about the time of death
rationale: Sirach reminds the reader that death will not delay and Hades's covenant has not been disclosed; Ecclesiastes likewise says a person does not know his time and can be caught suddenly, without using the covenant expression.
source_text: Remember that death will not delay, and the covenant of Hades has not been shown to you.

target_units.text: For a person does not know his time: like fish caught in an evil net, and birds caught in a snare, so human beings are trapped at an evil time when it falls upon them suddenly.

relationship: close timely generosity while the hand can help
rationale: Sirach urges giving to a friend before death and according to one's strength; Proverbs likewise commands present help when the hand has means and warns against postponing it because the next day is unknown.
source_text: Before you die, do good to a friend; according to your strength, reach out and give to him.

target_units.text: Do not refrain from doing good to someone in need whenever your hand has the means to help.
Do not say, ‘Go away and come back; tomorrow I will give,’ when you are able to do good, for you do not know what the coming day will bring forth.

relationship: parallel enjoyment of one's available share in life
rationale: Sirach warns against missing a good day and one's share of good desire; Ecclesiastes likewise urges glad food, drink and shared life as one's portion beneath the sun.
source_text: Do not miss a good day, and do not let your share of a good desire pass you by.

target_units.text: Come, eat your bread with gladness and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already favored your deeds.
Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not be lacking on your head.

Enjoy life with the woman whom you have loved, all the days of your futile life that have been given you under the sun, all your futile days; for this is your share in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.

relationship: close toil passing to a successor
rationale: Sirach asks whether one's labor will be left for another's inheritance; Ecclesiastes likewise laments leaving the fruits of wise toil to a successor who did not perform it.
source_text: Will you not leave your labors to another, and your toils to the division of an inheritance?

target_units.text: I hated all my toil with which I toil beneath the sun, because I leave it to the person who comes after me.
Who knows whether he will be wise or foolish? Yet he has authority over all the toil with which I labored and acted wisely beneath the sun. This too is futility.
I turned to bid my heart farewell concerning all the toil with which I had labored beneath the sun,
for a person may toil with wisdom, knowledge and courage, yet will give his portion to someone who did not toil for it. This too is futility and a great evil.

relationship: parallel present enjoyment before Hades ends earthly activity
rationale: Sirach urges giving, receiving and enjoyment because luxury is not sought in Hades; Ecclesiastes likewise urges glad living and vigorous action before Hades, where work and knowledge are absent.
source_text: Give and receive, and beguile your soul, for in Hades there is no seeking luxury.

target_units.text: Come, eat your bread with gladness and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already favored your deeds.
Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not be lacking on your head.

Enjoy life with the woman whom you have loved, all the days of your futile life that have been given you under the sun, all your futile days; for this is your share in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your strength, for there is no deed, reckoning, knowledge or wisdom in Hades, where you are going.

relationship: close garment-like aging and mortality image
rationale: Sirach says flesh grows old like a garment under death's decree; Isaiah similarly says earth grows old like a garment and its inhabitants die, contrasting this with enduring divine salvation.
source_text: All flesh grows old like a garment, for the covenant from eternity is, “You will surely die.”

target_units.text: Lift your eyes to heaven and look at earth below. Heaven was made firm like smoke, but earth will grow old like a garment, and earth’s inhabitants will die like these. My salvation will last for ever, and My righteousness will never fail.

relationship: close succession of mortal generations
rationale: Sirach's falling and growing leaves illustrate one generation dying as another is born; Ecclesiastes likewise says a generation goes and a generation comes, without the leaf image.
source_text: Like flourishing foliage on a leafy tree—some it casts down, while other leaves it grows—so is a generation of flesh and blood: one dies, and another is born.

target_units.text: A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth stands for ever.

relationship: contrast between mortal makers and the enduring Creator
rationale: Sirach says a decaying work and its maker both depart; the psalm contrasts perishable, garment-like created works with the Lord who remains unchanged. The difference between human makers and God is explicit.
source_text: Every decaying work comes to an end, and its maker will depart with it.

target_units.text: At the beginning Thou, Lord, didst found the earth, and the heavens are works of Thy hands.
They will perish, but Thou wilt remain; all will grow old like a garment. Like a cloak Thou wilt change them, and they will be changed.
But Thou art the same, and Thy years will not fail.

relationship: parallel blessedness in sustained meditation
rationale: Sirach blesses meditation on wisdom; the psalm likewise blesses the person whose desire and day-and-night meditation are in the Lord's law.
source_text: Happy is the man who will meditate on wisdom and speak with his understanding,

target_units.text: Blessed is the man who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, and did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of pestilent men;
but his will is in the Lord’s law, and on His law he will meditate day and night.

relationship: parallel inward and searching attention to wisdom
rationale: Sirach directs the heart toward wisdom's ways and hidden things; Proverbs likewise directs heart and ear toward understanding and urges searching for it as for treasure.
source_text: who considers her ways in his heart and will reflect upon her hidden things.

target_units.text: your ear will obey wisdom, and you will apply your heart to understanding; you will also apply it to admonishing your son.
for if you call upon wisdom and give your voice to understanding, and seek perception with a loud voice,
and if you seek it like silver and search it out like treasures,
then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God.

relationship: parallel active pursuit of wisdom
rationale: Sirach imagines tracking wisdom along her paths; Proverbs similarly calls for urgent seeking and treasure-like searching, using a different pursuit image.
source_text: Go out after her like a tracker, and lie in wait on her paths.

target_units.text: for if you call upon wisdom and give your voice to understanding, and seek perception with a loud voice,
and if you seek it like silver and search it out like treasures,
then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God.

relationship: close listening at wisdom's entrance
rationale: Sirach depicts peering through wisdom's windows and listening at her doorways; personified wisdom in Proverbs likewise blesses the listener watching daily at her doors and entrances.
source_text: The one who peers through her windows will also listen at her doorways;

target_units.text: Happy is the man who will listen to me, and the person who will keep my ways, staying awake at my doors day by day, guarding the posts of my entrances.

relationship: close abiding beside wisdom's dwelling
rationale: Sirach pitches lodging and a tent peg near wisdom's house; Proverbs likewise pictures persistent attendance at her doors and entrance-posts, without the same tent details.
source_text: the one who lodges near her house will fix a tent peg in her walls.

target_units.text: Happy is the man who will listen to me, and the person who will keep my ways, staying awake at my doors day by day, guarding the posts of my entrances.

relationship: related welcome into wisdom's beneficial house
rationale: Sirach's tent beside wisdom offers lodging in good things; Proverbs likewise presents wisdom's built house and invitation to life-giving food and understanding, without describing the guest's tent.
source_text: He will pitch his tent beside her and lodge in a lodging of good things.

target_units.text: Wisdom built herself a house, and set seven pillars beneath it.
She slaughtered her own sacrificial animals, mixed her own wine in a mixing-bowl, and prepared her own table.
She sent her own servants, summoning with a lofty proclamation to the mixing-bowl, saying:
“Whoever is foolish, let him turn aside to me!” And to those lacking understanding she said:
“Come, eat of my loaves, and drink wine that I mixed for you.
Leave foolishness, and you will live; seek understanding, so that you may live, and set insight right in knowledge.”

relationship: close wisdom as a protective tree
rationale: Sirach places children in wisdom's shelter and the learner beneath her branches; Proverbs likewise calls wisdom a tree of life and a secure support for those holding and leaning upon her, without specifying children.
source_text: He will place his children in her shelter and spend the night beneath her branches.

target_units.text: She is a tree of life to all who hold her fast, and secure for those who lean on her as on the Lord.

relationship: related glorious shelter from heat
rationale: Sirach makes wisdom a shelter from heat and dwelling in glory; Isaiah similarly depicts glory-covered Zion as shade from heat and shelter, in a different setting.
source_text: He will be sheltered by her from the heat and lodge in her glory.

target_units.text: He will come, and it will be: a cloud will shade every place of Mount Zion and everything around her by day, and as of smoke and as of a light of fire burning by night; with all the glory it will be covered.
It will be shade from heat, shelter and concealment from harshness and rain.
