relationship: close wisdom gained by keeping divine instruction
rationale: Sirach joins gaining wisdom with holding fast to the law; Deuteronomy likewise calls keeping and doing God's ordinances Israel's wisdom and understanding.
source_text: The one who fears the Lord will do this, and the one who holds fast to the law will gain her.

target_units.text: Behold, I have shown you ordinances and judgments, as the Lord commanded me, that you should do so in the land whither you go to inherit it.

And you shall keep and do them; for this is your wisdom and understanding before all the nations, who shall hear all these ordinances and say: Behold, this great nation is a wise and understanding people.

relationship: close wisdom portrayed as a desired wife
rationale: Sirach says wisdom welcomes the learner like a wife of his youth; Wisdom's speaker likewise seeks her as a bride from youth. Sirach also adds the distinct mother image.
source_text: She will meet him like a mother and welcome him like a wife of his youth.

target_units.text: I loved her and sought her out from my youth, and sought to take her as my bride, and became a lover of her beauty.

relationship: close wisdom's nourishing invitation
rationale: Sirach has wisdom feed the learner bread of understanding and water of wisdom; personified wisdom in Proverbs likewise offers bread and drink leading away from foolishness toward understanding and life, using wine rather than water.
source_text: She will feed him bread of understanding and give him water of wisdom to drink.

target_units.text: “Come, eat of my loaves, and drink wine that I mixed for you.
Leave foolishness, and you will live; seek understanding, so that you may live, and set insight right in knowledge.”

relationship: close security through holding and leaning upon wisdom
rationale: Sirach says the person leaning on wisdom will not be shaken; Proverbs similarly calls her secure for those who hold and lean upon her.
source_text: He will lean upon her and certainly not be shaken; he will hold to her and certainly not be put to shame.

target_units.text: She is a tree of life to all who hold her fast, and secure for those who lean on her as on the Lord.

relationship: close public honor and authoritative speech through wisdom
rationale: Sirach describes wisdom raising a person above neighbors and opening his mouth in the assembly; Wisdom's speaker likewise expects public honor and an attentive audience when he speaks through her.
source_text: She will raise him above his neighbors and open his mouth in the midst of the assembly.

target_units.text: Through her I will have glory among the crowds, and, though young, honor among elders.
I will be found keen in judgment and will be admired in the sight of rulers.
When I am silent they will wait for me, and when I speak they will pay attention; if I speak at length, they will place a hand upon their mouth.

relationship: close wisdom's crown of rejoicing
rationale: Sirach promises a crown of rejoicing through wisdom; Proverbs likewise says honoring her brings a crown of graces and delight. The everlasting name is an additional Sirach promise.
source_text: He will find gladness and a crown of rejoicing, and inherit an everlasting name.

target_units.text: Fortify her, and she will exalt you; honor her so that she may embrace you,
so that she may give your head a crown of graces and shield you with a crown of delight.

relationship: close exclusion of sinful people from wisdom
rationale: Sirach says sinful people will not see wisdom; Wisdom likewise says she will not enter an evil-devising soul or dwell in a body indebted to sin.
source_text: People without understanding will certainly not gain her, and sinful men will certainly not see her.

target_units.text: For wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, nor will she dwell in a body indebted to sin.

relationship: parallel opposition between pride and wisdom
rationale: Sirach says wisdom is far from pride; Proverbs likewise contrasts insolence and dishonor with the humble mouth meditating on wisdom. Sirach additionally excludes lying people.
source_text: She is far from pride, and lying men will certainly not remember her.

target_units.text: Wherever insolence enters, dishonor is there too, but the mouth of the humble meditates on wisdom.

relationship: related rejection of religious speech detached from obedience
rationale: Sirach finds praise unfitting in a sinner's mouth; God in the psalm likewise questions a sinner reciting His decrees and covenant while hating instruction.
source_text: Praise is not fitting in a sinner’s mouth, because it was not sent from the Lord.

target_units.text: But to the sinner God said, “Why do you recount My decrees and take up My covenant through your mouth?
But you hated instruction and cast My words behind you.

relationship: close praise offered with understanding
rationale: Sirach says praise will be spoken in wisdom; the psalm likewise commands music to God with understanding, without repeating Sirach's promise that He will prosper it.
source_text: For praise will be spoken in wisdom, and the Lord will cause it to prosper.

target_units.text: Make music to our God, make music; make music to our King, make music.
For God is King of all the earth; make music with understanding.

relationship: close refusal to blame God for moral failure
rationale: Sirach forbids attributing falling away to the Lord, who does not do what He hates; James likewise forbids saying God tempts a person with evil.
source_text: Do not say, “Because of the Lord I fell away,” for He will not do the things He hates.

target_units.text: Let no one who is tempted say, “I am being tempted by God.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, and He Himself tempts no one.

relationship: close rejection of God as the source of sinful enticement
rationale: Sirach rejects the claim that God led a person astray; James likewise locates sinful temptation in one's own desire rather than God's action.
source_text: Do not say, “He Himself led me astray,” for He has no need of a sinful man.

target_units.text: Let no one who is tempted say, “I am being tempted by God.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, and He Himself tempts no one.
But each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own desire.
Then desire, after conceiving, gives birth to sin; and sin, when fully grown, gives birth to death.

relationship: close fear of the Lord expressed in hatred of evil
rationale: Sirach joins the Lord's hatred of abominations with the attitude of those fearing Him; Proverbs likewise says fear of the Lord hates injustice, arrogance and wicked ways.
source_text: The Lord has hated every abomination, and it is not loved by those who fear Him.

target_units.text: The fear of the Lord hates injustice, insolence and arrogance and the ways of wicked people; and I hate the perverted ways of evil people.

relationship: related human responsibility to choose a course before God
rationale: Sirach says the created human was left to his own deliberation; Deuteronomy likewise calls for choosing life through love and obedience. The link concerns moral choice, not an added comprehensive theory of freedom.
source_text: He Himself made the human being from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own deliberation.

target_units.text: I call heaven and earth to witness unto you this day: I have set before your face life and death, the blessing and the curse. Choose life, that you and your seed may live,

to love the Lord your God, to obey His voice, and to cleave unto Him; for this is your life and the length of your days, that you may dwell upon the land which the Lord sware unto your fathers, Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, to give unto them.

relationship: close willingness and practicable obedience
rationale: Sirach connects keeping commandments with willingness and faithful intent; Deuteronomy likewise says the command is near enough to do and sets out life through obedience.
source_text: If you are willing, you will keep the commandments; to act faithfully is a matter of good will.

target_units.text: The word is very near you, in your mouth, and in your heart, and in your hands, that you may do it.
Behold, I have set before your face this day life and death, good and evil.

If you obey the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you this day, to love the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His ordinances and His judgments, then you shall live and be many; and the Lord your God shall bless you in all the land into which you go to inherit it.

relationship: parallel alternatives placed before human choice
rationale: Sirach pictures fire and water set before the chooser; Deuteronomy similarly sets life and death before Israel and commands choosing life. The pairs are compared rather than declared identical images.
source_text: He has placed fire and water before you; toward whichever you wish, you will stretch out your hand.

target_units.text: Behold, I have set before your face this day life and death, good and evil.

If you obey the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you this day, to love the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His ordinances and His judgments, then you shall live and be many; and the Lord your God shall bless you in all the land into which you go to inherit it.
And if your heart turns aside, and you will not hearken, and you are led astray to bow down unto other gods and serve them,
I declare unto you this day that you shall surely perish, and you shall in no wise be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you, into which you are crossing the Jordan to inherit it.
I call heaven and earth to witness unto you this day: I have set before your face life and death, the blessing and the curse. Choose life, that you and your seed may live,

relationship: close life-and-death choice formula
rationale: Both set life and death before the human recipient and connect choice with its outcome; Deuteronomy expressly commands choosing life.
source_text: Before human beings are life and death, and whichever a person chooses will be given to him.

target_units.text: I call heaven and earth to witness unto you this day: I have set before your face life and death, the blessing and the curse. Choose life, that you and your seed may live,

relationship: close greatness of divine strength and understanding
rationale: Sirach celebrates the Lord's great wisdom and strong dominion; the psalm likewise joins His greatness and strength with understanding beyond number. Sirach adds explicit universal sight.
source_text: For the Lord’s wisdom is great; He is strong in dominion and sees all things.

target_units.text: Great is our Lord, and great is His strength; His understanding is beyond number.

relationship: close divine sight of deeds and regard for those who fear Him
rationale: Sirach joins God's eyes upon those fearing Him with knowledge of every deed; the psalm likewise joins seeing humanity, understanding all deeds and eyes upon those who fear Him.
source_text: His eyes are upon those who fear Him, and He Himself will know every human deed.

target_units.text: From heaven the Lord looked down; He saw all the sons of men.
From His prepared dwelling place He looked upon all who inhabit the earth.
He formed their hearts individually; He understands all their deeds.
A king is not saved through a great force, and a giant will not be saved by the abundance of his strength.
A horse is false for salvation, and by the abundance of its power it will not be saved.
Behold, the Lord’s eyes are upon those who fear Him, those who hope in His mercy,

relationship: parallel divine opposition to lawlessness
rationale: Sirach denies that God commands ungodliness or licenses sin; the psalm likewise says God does not desire lawlessness and will not receive an evildoer, without using the same command-and-license terms.
source_text: He commanded no one to act ungodly, and He gave no one license to sin.

target_units.text: For Thou art not a God who desires lawlessness, nor will an evildoer sojourn with Thee.

relationship: close useless multitude of ungodly offspring
rationale: Sirach warns against desiring many useless, ungodly children; Wisdom likewise calls the prolific multitude of the ungodly useless and without a secure root.
source_text: Do not desire a multitude of useless children, or rejoice in ungodly sons.

target_units.text: But the prolific multitude of the ungodly will be of no use; from illegitimate shoots it will not send a root deep down, nor establish a secure foundation.

relationship: parallel virtue valued above mere fertility
rationale: Sirach makes fear of the Lord the condition for rejoicing over many children; Wisdom similarly prefers virtuous childlessness to the ungodly's prolific but useless multitude.
source_text: Even if they multiply, do not rejoice in them unless the fear of the Lord is with them.

target_units.text: Childlessness with virtue is better, for immortality is in its remembrance, because it is recognized both by God and by human beings.
When it is present, people imitate it, and when it has departed, they long for it; throughout the age it marches crowned in triumph, having won the contest for undefiled prizes.
But the prolific multitude of the ungodly will be of no use; from illegitimate shoots it will not send a root deep down, nor establish a secure foundation.

relationship: close preference for virtuous childlessness over ungodly descendants
rationale: Sirach explicitly prefers dying childless to having ungodly children; Wisdom likewise calls childlessness with virtue better and denies the value of ungodly proliferation.
source_text: Do not trust in their life or rely on their multitude. For one is better than a thousand, and it is better to die childless than to have ungodly children.

target_units.text: Childlessness with virtue is better, for immortality is in its remembrance, because it is recognized both by God and by human beings.
When it is present, people imitate it, and when it has departed, they long for it; throughout the age it marches crowned in triumph, having won the contest for undefiled prizes.
But the prolific multitude of the ungodly will be of no use; from illegitimate shoots it will not send a root deep down, nor establish a secure foundation.

relationship: close one wise person's benefit to a city
rationale: Sirach says one understanding person can settle a city while lawless people bring desolation; Ecclesiastes likewise pictures one poor wise man delivering a city and warns that one sinner destroys much good.
source_text: For through one understanding person a city will be settled, but a tribe of lawless people will become desolate.

target_units.text: and he might find in it a poor wise man, who will deliver the city by his wisdom; yet no one remembered that poor man.
I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.
The words of the wise, heard quietly, are better than the shouting of rulers in follies.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner will destroy much good.

relationship: narrative example of fire in a rebellious assembly
rationale: Sirach recalls fire among sinners and wrath in a disobedient nation; Numbers supplies the Lord's fire consuming the assembled incense-offerers within the rebellion narrative.
source_text: In an assembly of sinners fire will be kindled, and in a disobedient nation wrath was kindled.

target_units.text: And fire went out from the Lord and consumed the two hundred fifty men presenting the incense.

relationship: close judgment of the ancient arrogant giants
rationale: Sirach recalls ancient giants rebelling in strength without receiving atonement; Wisdom likewise recalls arrogant giants perishing at the beginning while the world's hope survives on a raft.
source_text: He did not make atonement for the ancient giants, who rebelled in their strength.

target_units.text: For even at the beginning, when arrogant giants were perishing, the hope of the world took refuge on a raft and left to the age a seed for generation, steered by Thy hand.

relationship: close Sodom judged for arrogance
rationale: Sirach identifies Lot's neighbors as judged for pride; Ezekiel likewise names Sodom's arrogance, boasting and lawlessness before reporting her removal. The separately read Genesis 19 establishes the Lot setting.
source_text: He did not spare Lot’s neighbors, whom He loathed because of their pride.

target_units.text: Yet this was the lawlessness of your sister Sodom: arrogance. In fullness of bread and abundance of wine she and her daughters lived luxuriously. This belonged to her and her daughters, but they did not support the hand of the poor and needy.
They boasted greatly and committed acts of lawlessness before Me, and I removed them as I saw.

relationship: wilderness-generation judgment allusion
rationale: Sirach recalls the hardened six hundred thousand foot soldiers; Numbers announces death in the wilderness for the counted generation that grumbled. Exodus 12:37 supplies the separately read six-hundred-thousand departure count.
source_text: and likewise on the six hundred thousand foot soldiers gathered together in their hardness of heart.

target_units.text: How long with this evil congregation? They grumble before Me; I have heard the sons of Israel’s grumbling that they have directed against you.
Say to them, I live, says the Lord: I will certainly do to you just as you have spoken into My ears.
In this wilderness your bodies shall fall, with your entire registration and those of you counted from twenty years old and upward who grumbled against Me.
You shall certainly not enter the land over which I stretched out My hand to settle you upon it, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.

relationship: close mercy joined with refusal to acquit wrongdoing
rationale: Sirach pairs great atoning mercy with poured-out wrath and doubt that the stiff-necked will be acquitted; Exodus likewise joins abundant mercy and forgiveness with refusal to cleanse the guilty.
source_text: Even if there is one stiff-necked person, it is a wonder if he will be acquitted. For mercy and wrath are with Him; He is mighty in atonements and pours out wrath.

target_units.text: The Lord passed before him and proclaimed, “The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger, abundant in mercy and true,

preserving righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness, injustice, and sins, yet not cleansing the guilty, bringing the fathers’ lawlessness upon children and children’s children to the third and fourth generation.”

relationship: close divine judgment according to deeds
rationale: Sirach says God will judge a person according to deeds amid mercy and rebuke; Romans likewise describes repayment according to works with differing outcomes for perseverance and unrighteousness.
source_text: As His mercy is great, so also His rebuke is great; He will judge a man according to his deeds.

target_units.text: who will repay each according to his works:
to those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory and honor and incorruptibility, eternal life;
but to those acting from selfish ambition, who disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, wrath and fury,

relationship: parallel judgment preventing a plunderer's escape
rationale: Sirach says a sinner will not escape with his plunder; Habakkuk likewise announces that one who plundered nations will become their plunder. Sirach's promise about godly endurance is additional.
source_text: A sinner will not escape with his plunder, and a godly person’s endurance will certainly not be left behind.

target_units.text: Will not all these take up a parable against him and a riddle for his account? They will say, ‘Woe to the one multiplying for himself what is not his—how long?—and heavily weighting his collar!’
For suddenly those biting him will rise, and those plotting against you will awake; you will become their plunder.
Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

relationship: close divine recognition and repayment of almsgiving
rationale: Sirach says every almsgiving receives room and each person receives according to deeds; Jesus likewise promises that the Father sees secret almsgiving and repays it.
source_text: He will make room for every act of almsgiving; each person will receive according to his deeds.

target_units.text: But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,
so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will repay you.

relationship: close denial of hiding from the God who fills creation
rationale: Sirach rejects the excuse that one small life is hidden within immeasurable creation; Jeremiah likewise asks whether anyone can hide from the Lord who fills heaven and earth.
source_text: Do not say, “I will be hidden from the Lord; who will remember me from on high? Among a numerous people I will certainly not be known, for what is my soul in the immeasurable creation?”

target_units.text: I am a God drawing near, says the Lord, and not a God far away.
If a person hides in hidden places, will I not see him? Do I not fill the heaven and the earth? says the Lord.

relationship: parallel cosmic shaking at divine visitation
rationale: Sirach describes heaven, abyss and earth shaken at God's visitation; the psalm likewise describes earth and mountain foundations shaking as God descends in anger.
source_text: Behold, heaven and the heaven of heaven, the abyss and the earth will be shaken at His visitation.

target_units.text: And the earth was shaken and began to tremble; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken because God was angry with them.
Smoke rose in His anger, and fire from His face set things ablaze; coals were kindled from Him.
And He bent heaven and came down, and gloom was beneath His feet.

relationship: close trembling of foundations and mountains
rationale: Sirach makes mountains and earth's foundations tremble at God's look; the psalm likewise joins trembling earth with shaken mountain foundations under divine anger.
source_text: Together the mountains and the foundations of the earth are shaken with trembling when He looks upon them.

target_units.text: And the earth was shaken and began to tremble; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken because God was angry with them.

relationship: related failure to understand divine works
rationale: Sirach's questions about hearts considering God's ways culminate in the verdict of folly at 16:23; the psalm likewise contrasts God's deep works and reasonings with the senseless person's failure to understand.
source_text: Yet no heart will consider these things, and who will ponder His ways?

target_units.text: How great Thy works have become, Lord; Thy reasonings have grown very deep.
A senseless man will not know, and one without understanding will not understand these things:

relationship: related skeptical questioning of a delayed divine promise
rationale: Sirach's questions about waiting and the distant covenant are followed by a judgment of foolish reasoning; Peter likewise reports scoffers questioning the promise of the Lord's coming. The specific promises and settings differ.
source_text: Who will announce works of righteousness? Who will wait? For the covenant is far away.

target_units.text: knowing this first: in the last days scoffers will come with scoffing, walking according to their own desires,
and saying, “Where is the promise of His coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it was from the beginning of creation.”

relationship: close foolish failure to understand God's works
rationale: Sirach identifies the preceding reasoning as that of someone deficient in heart; the psalm likewise calls the person unable to understand God's deep works senseless and without understanding.
source_text: Someone deficient in heart thinks these things; a foolish and wandering man thinks foolish things.

target_units.text: How great Thy works have become, Lord; Thy reasonings have grown very deep.
A senseless man will not know, and one without understanding will not understand these things:

relationship: close teacher's appeal to a child's attentive heart
rationale: Sirach asks the child to listen, learn and attend with the heart; Proverbs similarly asks the son to attend to words, apply the ear and keep them in the heart.
source_text: Listen to me, child, and learn knowledge; attend to my words with your heart.

target_units.text: Son, attend to my utterance; apply your ear to my words,
so that your springs do not fail you; keep them in your heart,
for there is life for those who find them and healing for all flesh.

relationship: creation example of assigned functions from the beginning
rationale: Sirach says God distinguished His works' portions from their making; Genesis illustrates that ordering by assigning the lights their functions in day, night and seasons.
source_text: By the Lord’s judgment His works have existed from the beginning; from their making He distinguished their portions.

target_units.text: And God said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth and to divide the day from the night. Let them serve for signs and seasons, for days and years.
And let them be lights in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth.” And it was so.
And God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; He made the stars also.
And God set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth,
to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good.

relationship: close enduring establishment of created works
rationale: Sirach says God ordered His works and their dominions forever; the psalm likewise joins creation by command with their establishment for the age and a command that does not pass away. The absence of hunger and weariness is Sirach's additional description.
source_text: He ordered His works for ever and their dominions through their generations. They neither hungered nor grew weary, and they did not cease from their tasks.

target_units.text: Let them praise the Lord’s name, for He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created.
He established them for the age and for the age of the age; He set a command, and it will not pass away.

relationship: parallel creation obeying divine command
rationale: Sirach says the works will not disobey God's word; the psalm likewise depicts earthly elements and storm wind fulfilling His word, without describing their relation to neighboring works.
source_text: None crowded out its neighbor, and for ever they will not disobey His word.

target_units.text: Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps,
fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind—all fulfilling His word,

relationship: close earth filled with God's provision
rationale: Sirach says the Lord filled earth with good things; the psalm likewise joins earth filled with His possession and living creatures filled with goodness when His hand opens.
source_text: After these things the Lord looked upon the earth and filled it with His good things.

target_units.text: How great Thy works have become, Lord! Thou madest all things in wisdom; the earth was filled with Thy possession.
Here is the sea, great and spacious; there are creeping things without number, living creatures small with great.
There ships pass, and this dragon, which Thou didst form to play with it.
All wait for Thee to give them food at the right time.
When Thou givest to them, they will gather; when Thou openest Thy hand, all things will be filled with goodness.

relationship: close creaturely life and return to dust
rationale: Sirach joins earth's living creatures with their return to it; the psalm likewise describes creatures returning to dust when breath is taken and renewed creation through God's Spirit.
source_text: He covered its face with the life of every living creature, and to it they return.

target_units.text: When Thou turnest Thy face away, they will be troubled. Thou wilt take back their breath, and they will fail and return to their dust.
Thou wilt send Thy Spirit, and they will be created, and Thou wilt renew the face of the earth.

relationship: close earth-origin and earth-return formula
rationale: Sirach says the human was created from earth and returned to it; Genesis likewise declares the human earth, taken from earth and returning to earth.
source_text: The Lord created a human being from earth and returned him to it again.

target_units.text: By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for earth you are, and unto earth you shall return.

relationship: close numbered lifespan and appointed limit
rationale: Sirach gives humanity numbered days and an appointed time; Job likewise speaks of months numbered with God and a boundary that cannot be exceeded. The authority over earthly things is not repeated there.
source_text: He gave them numbered days and an appointed time, and He gave them authority over the things upon it.

target_units.text: Even if his life on earth is one day, his months are numbered with Thee; Thou didst set a time, and he will certainly not go beyond it.

relationship: close creation in God's image
rationale: Sirach says God made humans according to His image; Genesis likewise explicitly narrates humanity's making in God's image and likeness.
source_text: He clothed them with strength like His own and made them according to His image.

target_units.text: And God said, “Let Us make man in Our image and likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the cattle, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”
And God made man; in the image of God He made him; male and female He made them.

relationship: close animals' fear and humanity's dominion
rationale: Sirach says fear of human beings was placed upon flesh with dominion over beasts and birds; Genesis likewise places human dread upon beasts, birds and other creatures given into human hands.
source_text: He placed the fear of the human being upon all flesh and granted dominion over beasts and winged creatures.

target_units.text: The dread and fear of you shall fall upon every wild beast of the earth, every bird of heaven, everything that moves upon the earth, and every fish of the sea. Into your hands I have given them.

relationship: close divine gift of hearing and sight
rationale: Sirach attributes eyes and ears, among other capacities, to God; Proverbs likewise calls the hearing ear and seeing eye the Lord's works, without listing all Sirach's other faculties.
source_text: He gave them deliberation, a tongue and eyes, ears and a heart for understanding.

target_units.text: An ear hears and an eye sees; both are works of the Lord.

relationship: related divine presentation of good and evil
rationale: Sirach says God supplied discerning knowledge and showed good and evil; Deuteronomy likewise places life, death, good and evil before Israel with instruction for obedience, within a particular covenant address.
source_text: He filled them with discerning knowledge and showed them good things and evil things.

target_units.text: Behold, I have set before your face this day life and death, good and evil.

If you obey the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you this day, to love the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His ordinances and His judgments, then you shall live and be many; and the Lord your God shall bless you in all the land into which you go to inherit it.

relationship: close holy-name praise and recounting divine works
rationale: Sirach joins praising the holy name with recounting God's great works; the psalm likewise joins calling on His name, announcing His works and recounting His wonders.
source_text: and they will praise the holy name, so that they may recount the greatness of His works.

target_units.text: Hallelujah. Give thanks to the Lord and call upon His name; announce His works among the nations.
Sing to Him and make music to Him; recount all His wonders.
Be praised in His holy name; let the heart of those seeking the Lord rejoice.

relationship: close law given as an inheritance
rationale: Sirach calls the law of life an inheritance; Deuteronomy likewise calls Moses's commanded law an inheritance for Jacob's assemblies.
source_text: He added knowledge to them and gave them the law of life as an inheritance.

target_units.text: the law which Moses commanded us, an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob.

relationship: close everlasting covenant established for Israel
rationale: Sirach recalls an everlasting covenant and revealed judgments; the psalm likewise says God remembered His covenant forever and established it for Israel as an everlasting covenant.
source_text: He established an everlasting covenant with them and showed them His judgments.

target_units.text: He remembered His covenant for ever, the word He commanded for a thousand generations,
which He covenanted with Abraham, and His oath to Isaac;
He established it for Jacob as an ordinance and for Israel as an everlasting covenant,

relationship: close glory seen and divine voice heard
rationale: Sirach describes the people's eyes seeing great glory and their ears hearing God's voice; Deuteronomy recounts the assembly hearing the voice from fire and affirming that God showed His glory.
source_text: Their eyes saw the greatness of glory, and their ear heard the glory of His voice.

target_units.text: These words the Lord spoke unto all your assembly on the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, with darkness, gloom, tempest, and a great voice; and He added no more. And He wrote them upon two tablets of stone, and gave them unto me.
And it came to pass, when you heard the voice out of the midst of the fire, and the mountain burned with fire, that you drew near unto me, all the heads of your tribes and your elders,
and said: Behold, the Lord our God has shown us His glory, and we have heard His voice out of the midst of the fire. This day we have seen that God speaks with man, and he lives.

relationship: close prohibition of injustice toward one's neighbor
rationale: Sirach says God warned against injustice and commanded concerning neighbors; Leviticus provides explicit commands against wronging, robbing, unjustly judging, hating and taking vengeance against a neighbor.
source_text: He said to them, “Beware of every injustice,” and commanded each of them concerning the neighbor.

target_units.text: You shall not wrong your neighbour, neither shall you rob; and the wages of the hired worker shall in no wise remain with you overnight until morning.
You shall not speak evil of the deaf, neither shall you put a stumbling block before the blind; and you shall fear the Lord your God; I am the Lord your God.
You shall do no injustice in judgment; you shall not favour the person of the poor, neither shall you admire the person of the mighty; you shall judge your neighbour in righteousness.
You shall not go about deceitfully among your nation; you shall not conspire against the blood of your neighbour; I am the Lord your God.
You shall not hate your brother in your mind; you shall surely reprove your neighbour, and you shall not bear sin because of him.
And your hand shall not take vengeance, neither shall you remain angry with the sons of your people; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself; I am the Lord.

relationship: close human ways continually before God's eyes
rationale: Both say human ways lie before God's eyes; Proverbs adds that He watches every track, corresponding to Sirach's denial that those ways are hidden.
source_text: Their ways are continually before Him; they will not be hidden from His eyes.

target_units.text: For a man’s ways are before God’s eyes, and He watches all his tracks.

relationship: close division of nations and Israel as the Lord's portion
rationale: Sirach contrasts appointed national rulers with Israel as God's own portion; Deuteronomy likewise describes national bounds according to God's angels and Jacob as the Lord's portion.
source_text: He appointed a ruler for each nation, but Israel is the Lord’s portion.

target_units.text: When the Most High divided the nations, when He scattered the sons of Adam, He set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.
And His people Jacob became the portion of the Lord; Israel, the measured lot of His inheritance.

relationship: parallel complete divine observation of human deeds
rationale: Sirach makes human works visible before God and His eyes constant upon their ways; the psalm likewise says He sees earth's inhabitants and understands all their deeds, without the sun comparison.
source_text: All their works are like the sun before Him, and His eyes are continually upon their ways.

target_units.text: From heaven the Lord looked down; He saw all the sons of men.
From His prepared dwelling place He looked upon all who inhabit the earth.
He formed their hearts individually; He understands all their deeds.

relationship: close sins not hidden from God's eyes
rationale: Sirach says human injustices and sins are unhidden before the Lord; Jeremiah likewise explicitly denies that their ways or injustices are concealed from His eyes.
source_text: Their injustices were not hidden from Him, and all their sins are before the Lord.

target_units.text: Because My eyes are upon all their ways, and their wrongdoings were not hidden before My eyes.

relationship: related divine remembrance of almsgiving
rationale: Sirach compares almsgiving with a seal preserved before God; the angel likewise says Cornelius's alms have ascended as a memorial before Him, without repeating the pupil-of-the-eye comparison.
source_text: A man’s almsgiving is like a seal with Him, and He will guard human kindness like the pupil of an eye.

target_units.text: He stared at him in fear and said, “What is it, sir?” The angel said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.

relationship: close recompense returning upon the doer's head
rationale: Sirach says God will return recompense upon people's heads; Obadiah likewise announces action repaid upon the doer's own head in the day of the Lord.
source_text: After these things He will rise and repay them; He will return their recompense upon their head.

target_units.text: For the day of the Lord is near against all the nations. Just as you acted, so it will be for you; your recompense will be repaid upon your own head.

relationship: parallel divine opportunity for repentance
rationale: Sirach says God gives repentant people a way back and renewed courage; Wisdom likewise finds hope in God's gift of repentance and His provision of time and room to leave evil.
source_text: Yet He gave a way back to those who repent and encouraged those whose endurance was failing.

target_units.text: Through such works Thou didst teach Thy people that the righteous person must love humanity, and make Thy sons hopeful, because Thou givest repentance for sins.
For if Thou didst punish the enemies of Thy children, who were liable to death, with such attention and leniency, giving times and room through which they might be freed from evil,

relationship: close return to God with abandoned sins and petition
rationale: Sirach commands return to the Lord, leaving sins and petitioning Him; Isaiah likewise joins seeking and calling upon God with abandoning wicked ways and returning for mercy.
source_text: Return to the Lord and leave sins behind; petition Him face to face and lessen your stumbling.

target_units.text: Seek God, and when you find Him, call upon Him; and when He draws near to you,
let the ungodly forsake his ways, and the lawless man his counsels; and let him return to the Lord, and he will receive mercy; for He will abundantly forgive your sins.

relationship: close repentance as turning away from injustice
rationale: Sirach commands return to the Most High and rejection of injustice and abomination; Ezekiel likewise commands turning from impieties and casting them away in a renewed heart and spirit.
source_text: Come back to the Most High, turn away from injustice, and hate abomination intensely.

target_units.text: I will judge you, each according to his way, house of Israel, says the Lord. Turn back and turn away from all your impieties, and they will not become a punishment of injustice for you.
Cast away from yourselves all your impieties with which you acted impiously against Me, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why are you dying, house of Israel?

relationship: close question about thanksgiving in Hades
rationale: Both ask who in Hades will give God thanks or praise, contrasting death's silence with the living person's appeal to God.
source_text: Who in Hades will praise the Most High in place of the living who give acknowledgment?

target_units.text: For in death there is no one who remembers Thee; and in Hades, who will give Thee thanks?

relationship: close living praise contrasted with the dead
rationale: Sirach says thanksgiving perishes from the dead while the living praise; Isaiah likewise denies praise in Hades and assigns blessing to the living.
source_text: From the dead, as from one who does not exist, thanksgiving perishes; the living and healthy will praise the Lord.

target_units.text: For those in Hades will not praise Thee, nor will the dead bless Thee, nor will those in Hades hope for Thy mercy.
The living will bless Thee, as I do. For from today I will have children who will announce Thy righteousness,

relationship: close abundant mercy for those returning to God
rationale: Sirach celebrates mercy and atonement for those who return; Isaiah likewise promises mercy and abundant forgiveness to the ungodly who abandon their ways and return to the Lord.
source_text: How great is the Lord’s mercy and His atonement for those who return to Him!

target_units.text: let the ungodly forsake his ways, and the lawless man his counsels; and let him return to the Lord, and he will receive mercy; for He will abundantly forgive your sins.

relationship: related limitation of mortal access to unending life
rationale: Sirach says humanity cannot possess everything because it is not immortal; Genesis narrates exclusion from the tree that would enable living forever, without restating Sirach's whole claim about having everything.
source_text: For human beings cannot have everything, because a son of man is not immortal.

target_units.text: And God said, “Behold, Adam has become as one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he stretch forth his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever—”
And the Lord God sent him out of the garden of delight to till the earth from which he had been taken.
And He drove Adam out and settled him opposite the garden of delight. And He stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns about, to guard the way to the tree of life.

relationship: related celestial comparison exposing human frailty
rationale: Sirach contrasts even the bright sun's failure with flesh and blood conceiving evil; Bildad similarly contrasts the moon and stars' limitations with mortal impurity. The speakers and celestial objects are distinguished rather than equated.
source_text: What is brighter than the sun? Yet even it fails; and flesh and blood will conceive evil.

target_units.text: For how will a mortal be righteous before the Lord? Or who, being born of woman, could cleanse himself?
If He gives the moon a command, it does not shine; the stars are not pure before Him.
Leave it, then: a human is decay, and a son of humanity a worm.”

relationship: close earth-and-ashes description of humanity before God
rationale: Sirach contrasts God's heavenly survey with humans as earth and ashes; Abraham uses the same earth-and-ashes description while addressing the Lord, without the heavenly-height clause.
source_text: He Himself surveys the power of the height of heaven, but all human beings are earth and ashes.

target_units.text: And Abraham answered and said, “Now I have begun to speak to the Lord, though I am earth and ashes.
